https://www.timeshighereducation.com/cam.text: How to navigate multilingualism in global online classrooms Virtual international collaboration can develop intercultural competence and critical thinking skills. Here are strategies that help make these experiences valuable Internationalisation at home Online learning University course design and delivery Feature article Latin America Francisco Alberto Núñez Tapia CETYS Universidad 6 Aug 2026 1 Top of page Main text More on this topic image credit: [Jacob Wackerhausen] Getty Images . Created in partnership with Created in partnership with You may also like Five pillars of collaborative online learning Questions to ask when designing collaborative online learning experiences 4 minute read AI-proof project-based assessments by making them context-specific 4 minute read Popular resources 1 How to apply virtual reality to enhance learning experiences 2 Campus webinar: How will HE keep up with digitalisation? 3 Four ways to help international students’ understanding 4 AI literacy cannot be bolted on to first-year courses 5 Campus webinar: Lessons in academic profile building A scene has become increasingly common in my classroom, particularly in global industrial engineering and international business programmes. Students log into a shared virtual space knowing that they will soon interact with peers from the United States, Poland or Ukraine. Cameras turn on, microphones are tested and suddenly, the classroom expands beyond its physical boundaries. What follows is not simply a discussion in English, but a meeting of perspectives. In that moment, the benefits of multilingualism in university classrooms become clear. In these environments, teaching in English is no longer about language acquisition . Most of my students already communicate effectively in English. The real challenge lies in helping them to use that shared language to collaborate across cultures , interpret different perspectives and engage in meaningful dialogue. Students quickly realise that speaking the same language does not guarantee universal meanings. Concepts such as ethics, leadership, sustainability or social responsibility are interpreted through different social and institutional lenses. Consequently, one of the most valuable learning outcomes emerges from the need to navigate these differences. Rather than focusing on linguistic correctness, students are challenged to clarify, negotiate and sometimes rethink their assumptions to be understood. Designing collaboration beyond borders These dynamics become especially visible through collaborative online international learning (COIL) and internationalisation at home initiatives. Recently, students at my institution have collaborated with global peers on comparative analyses, presentations and problem-solving projects. In these settings, while English serves as a shared communication platform, the learning itself is the result of the diversity of perspectives. Classroom dynamics shift significantly: From teacher-student interactions to global peer interactions Students compare perspectives and reflect critically on their own assumptions Students develop intercultural competence alongside communication skills, both increasingly essential in global professional environments. Four strategies that strengthen multilingual virtual collaboration Structure interactions: international collaboration does not happen automatically. Debates , collaborative projects and guided discussions encourage students to explain concepts, compare realities and engage meaningfully with others rather than remain passive participants. Combine synchronous and asynchronous participation: digital collaboration improves when we balance live interaction with reflective participation. Tools such as Zoom, VoiceThread and Trello allow students to engage both in real time and asynchronously through complementary learning activities. For example, Zoom breakout rooms can be used for small-group debates, collaborative case analyses and intercultural interaction before students share their conclusions with the wider group. VoiceThread enables students to post short video or audio reflections on course topics and respond to peers across institutions, creating space for more deliberate participation, particularly for those who need additional time to formulate ideas in English. Trello serves as a shared project workspace where teams assign responsibilities, monitor progress, exchange sources and provide peer feedback while developing collaborative presentations or research projects. Together, these activities create a continuous cycle of interaction, reflection and collaboration that extends beyond scheduled class meetings and encourages more inclusive participation in multilingual settings. Spotlight guide: Support student success in the multilingual classroom Eleven ways to support international students who use English as a second language A universal design approach to teaching multilingual students Focus assessment on ideas, not language perfection: An important lesson from multilingual collaboration is that fluency alone does not guarantee effective communication. Assessment should prioritise clarity of ideas, analytical depth and engagement with multiple perspectives rather than grammatical perfection alone. For example, in international business courses, mixed international teams analyse topics such as corporate sustainability, ethical decision-making or market differences across countries. Students should be evaluated on the strength of their arguments, their ability to support claims with evidence and the extent to which they engage with perspectives contributed by international peers. In industrial engineering courses, students collaborate on comparative analyses of production systems or process-improvement challenges, where assessment focuses on problem-solving, justification of proposed solutions and effective teamwork across cultural contexts. Minor grammatical errors do not substantially affect grades when communication remains clear and ideas are well developed. This approach encourages students to take intellectual risks, participate more confidently and focus on building meaningful intercultural dialogue rather than striving for linguistic perfection. Design assignments around collaborative problem-solving: project-based learning works particularly well in international virtual environments because it allows students to apply concepts locally while collaborating globally. Comparative analysis, case studies and collaborative research projects encourage students to connect classroom concepts with real-world challenges while working across cultural and institutional contexts. One activity that works particularly well is a comparative sustainability project involving mixed international teams. Students work across universities to analyse how their respective countries tackle sustainability challenges such as water management, renewable energy adoption or corporate social responsibility. During synchronous Zoom sessions, teams discuss local realities and identify key differences, while asynchronous collaboration through Trello and shared documents allows them to exchange sources, develop comparative analyses and prepare joint presentations. Rather than search for a single “correct” solution, students learn to explain why different approaches emerge from distinct social, economic and institutional contexts. This project consistently leads to richer discussions, stronger critical thinking and a deeper appreciation of the value of interdisciplinary and intercultural collaboration. Multilingualism as an academic asset Online international collaboration also highlights the value of translanguaging practices . Even when English remains the primary language of communication, students naturally draw on their broader linguistic repertoires to process information, clarify concepts and support one another. This movement between languages strengthens understanding and reinforces multilingualism as an academic asset. Ultimately, the multilingual university is defined not by the number of languages spoken, but by the interactions those languages make possible. Teaching in this context is not about instructing students in a language they already know, but about guiding them to use that language to engage with the world, collaborate across cultures and develop the competencies required for an increasingly interconnected society. Francisco Alberto Núñez Tapia is a research professor at the College of Social Sciences and Humanities, CETYS University, Mexicali Campus. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Voters at city hall in Anchorage, Alaska, on 4 November 2024. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Alaska Man in prison in New York advances in primary for Alaska’s US House seat Democrat Eric Hafner, to be released in 2036, also ran for seat in 2024, securing spot on that general election ballot Associated Press Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.14 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 19.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man who is serving time in a federal prison in New York advanced on Wednesday from the primary for Alaska ’s lone US House seat. Eric Hafner, a registered Democrat, also ran for the seat in 2024 and secured a spot on the general election ballot that November despite a challenge brought by the Alaska Democratic party. Hafner pleaded guilty in 2022 to charges of making threats against police officers, judges and others. He is set to be released in 2036. The leading candidates in the race are the incumbent, Republican Nick Begich, and independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisher and retired educator. Hafner’s success in the primary as one of the candidates moving on to the general election is almost certain to draw another legal challenge because the US constitution requires candidates to live in the state they will represent at the time of the election. In the candidate information he filed with the state, he listed the same Box Elder, South Dakota, mailing address and New York phone number as his mother, Carol Hafner. Neither has any apparent ties to Alaska. Carol Hafner also is a failed prior candidate and ran again this year, this time in the state’s US Senate primary. Under Alaska’s election system, the top four primary finishers advance to the general election regardless of party affiliation. Eric Hafner received 5,757 votes after 93% of ballots had been counted. That was far behind the third-place candidate, Democrat Matt Schultz. But Schultz withdrew from the general election and was ineligible to advance. It remained too early to call the fourth-place finisher. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Top row, from left: Britons James Henderson, James Kirby and John Chapman were killed in the April 2024 Israeli strike on their aid convoy. The other victims were, bottom row, from left: Damian Sobol, Lalzawmi Frankcom, Jacob Flickinger and Saifeddin Abutaha. Composite: World Central Kitchen/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Top row, from left: Britons James Henderson, James Kirby and John Chapman were killed in the April 2024 Israeli strike on their aid convoy. The other victims were, bottom row, from left: Damian Sobol, Lalzawmi Frankcom, Jacob Flickinger and Saifeddin Abutaha. Composite: World Central Kitchen/Getty Images Israel-Gaza war ‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike Exclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tactic Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workers Matan Cohen in Jerusalem, and Julian Borger Fri 4 Sep 2026 20.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Seven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows. A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery to Gaza . Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed. The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route. However, interviews with senior Israeli officers involved in the incident or familiar with the official Israel investigation suggest it glossed over the role played in the killings by a common IDF practice used to designate targets, which endangers aid workers and civilians in general, especially when combined with the army’s open-ended mission to end Hamas’s civil control in Gaza. Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workers Read more More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military in the three years of the Gaza war. The army’s own internal data suggests more than three-quarters of the dead have been civilians. The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, said the WCK workers became potential targets after they had a brief encounter, lasting just minutes, with armed guards assumed to be from Hamas (an assumption later shown to be groundless). He deemed them to have “mixed together” with alleged Hamas militants, where mixing together was defined as being “near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on”. Asked whether the presence of armed men made the entire convoy a target, Mendel replied: “Certainly.” He concluded: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.” View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the Israeli airstrike on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza. Military prosecutors have ruled out criminal charges over the attack that claimed seven lives. Photograph: Ahmed Zakot/Reuters Mendel was referring to a general policy of haflala , “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association. The manner in which haflala is to be applied in a given sector is often conveyed in a commander’s mission brief delivered verbally to other officers. He said his unit had been commended by the army hierarchy for its involvement in several strikes on what were deemed to be Hamas attempted commandeering of aid. “They applauded us and were pleased with our action,” he said. The difference in the WCK incident was that foreign nationals were killed, he said. “That’s the whole difference. Not a substantive difference.” First location map and timeline When the WCK convoy was destroyed, it was nowhere near Israeli troops. Several Israeli officers familiar with the incident said the strikes were not ordered on the basis of an imminent threat to Israeli lives, but to fulfil the mission to thwart Hamas attempts to control aid deliveries. 2nd location map and timeline The IDF was approached for comment on the issues raised by the airstrikes and subsequent investigations but had not responded three days after the request. The WCK said the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings was “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. “At the time of the lethal attacks, our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” the WCK said. “The IDF had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.” Britain, Australia and Canada denounced the prosecutor’s decision as “shameful”, saying they would “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the slain aid workers. The UK opened an inquest in 2024 into the deaths of the three British team members: James Kirby, James Henderson and John Chapman. Saifeddin Abutaha, a Palestinian, Australian Zomi Frankcom , Damian Sobol, a Pole, and a dual Canadian-US citizen, Jacob Flickinger, were the other victims. The UK inquest was adjourned pending the outcome of the Israeli investigation. View image in fullscreen The funeral in Bristol of James Kirby, 47, in May 2024. Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images Mendel, who is the only officer of such high rank to have been dismissed for his actions in the Gaza war, has been portrayed in army command briefings as a rogue operator. Questions have been raised about a political motive. Mendel is a settler who is reported to have been one of the 130 signatories of a 20 January 2024 letter to the IDF calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted. However, the way the Israeli army operates in Gaza – rules of engagement are made contingent on local circumstances and passed on, often verbally, down the chain of command – gives officers at Mendel’s level wide discretion in subjective judgments as to who is a “terrorist” and therefore a target. An IDF officer familiar with the WCK killings said that given the circumstances and the standing IDF procedures, the overwhelming majority of officers would have acted in the same way. “There were armed men next to them,” the officer said. “If you took qualified people and put them on the call, in 90% of cases this is what would have happened,” the officer said. “In my guess, 99% of the time the first bomb would have been dropped; 90% of the time the second; 80% of the time the third.” Reserve Brigadier General Oren Solomon, the battle manager of Gaza Division, said that a mistake had been made in determining that an armed man had entered one of the vehicles, but added that once that error had been committed, the incrimination procedure led inevitably to the three missile strikes. “If I incriminated this vehicle beforehand as Hamas — anyone who escapes from it and enters another vehicle: death comes,” Brig Gen Solomon said. “Together with him they will die. That meets the incrimination rules, no problem.” A senior officer involved in the initial Israeli military investigation into the WCK case, argued Mendel overstepped in interpreting the rules of incrimination. “You can’t incriminate 20 people if there’s one armed,” he said. The officer argued that the first strike could have been justified by the initial misidentification, even at the cost of citizen casualties, but not the subsequent missiles. “You struck someone you suspected, a vehicle you suspected had an armed man in it. The moment two people came out, nobody with a weapon, the second and third strikes are contrary to orders because you don’t know whom you’re striking,” he said. The other systemic factor that contributed to the deaths of the seven aid workers, and potentially countless more civilians, was one of the missions given to the army in Gaza by Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government: to destroy Hamas’s influence and control. That meant anyone deemed to be involved in – or assisting – the Hamas administration, including by distributing aid, could find themselves in the sights of an Israeli drone operator. “I remind you that part of our mission was to crush Hamas’s ability to govern,” Mendel said. “Part of the mission was to hit that [Hamas-controlled aid deliveries], and we hit it.”” Interviews with IDF officers suggest there was a widespread belief in the ranks that Hamas had wrested control of the bulk of aid deliveries into Gaza. That assumption was unfounded, later analysis showed. It was a period of widespread hunger caused by an Israeli blockade, when food convoys were being mobbed by desperate civilians, criminal gangs and Hamas militia. The belief that Hamas hijacks were widespread meant that the appearance of armed men in proximity to the WCK vehicle in April 2024 fitted a “pattern of activity” that helped incriminate the whole convoy in the eyes of Mendel and his unit. The IDF officer familiar with the incident said it was common practice to designate any armed man in Gaza as Hamas or a “terrorist”, as Mendel did. The officer added: “How you define that it’s Hamas – he’s in proximity to weapons, and because he touches the trucks, and because he does all sorts of things that look as if he’s going to take over the trucks.” The role of the incrimination principle in the WCK killings shows how it has become a factor in the historically high proportion of civilians killed in the Gaza war. This sits alongside the routine acceptance of high “collateral damage” in the targeting of Hamas militants, the designation of large and shifting areas as free-fire zones, and the deliberate levelling of neighbourhoods to prevent the return of Palestinian communities. The common factor is that constraints on targeting were minimised in the interests of an open-ended mission. Since the start of the war in 2023, no Israeli soldier has been convicted of wrongful death or war crimes in Gaza operations. “I came to defeat Hamas,” Mendel said. “If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing.” He also dismissed the significance of the killings. “I think it’s an idiotic side event,” Mendel said. “It really isn’t a serious event.” Explore more on these topics Israel-Gaza war Israel Gaza Palestine Middle East and north Africa Benjamin Netanyahu news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://english.news.cn/20261102/04112c2.text: Hungarian fighter jets escort passenger plane after bomb threat forces it to divert to Budapest: official Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-11-02 21:45:30 This file photo taken on Oct. 30, 2026 shows Wizz Air aircrafts at Liszt Ferenc International Airport in Budapest, Hungary. (Xinhua/Hu Zhixuan) BUDAPEST, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- Hungarian Gripen fighter jets were scrambled on Monday to escort a Wizz Air passenger plane to Budapest after a bomb threat forces the plane to divert, Hungarian Defense Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said. The aircraft, which was scheduled to fly from London to Sofia, was forced to divert and requested a permission to land at Budapest's Liszt Ferenc International Airport, the minister said in a Facebook post. The incident triggered a NATO air policing ALPHA alert, prompting the Hungarian Armed Forces to deploy Gripen fighter jets within minutes to ensure the passenger plane's safe landing. The fighter jets returned to their base in Kecskemet, central Hungary, and the police took over the response on the ground. ■

https://www.politico.eu/article/5-labour.text: LONDON — Keir Starmer’s failed attempt at welfare reform was the beginning of the end of his premiership. Andy Burnham needs to avoid a similar fate. The new prime minister’s own effort to tackle a rapid surge in working-age sickness and disability benefit claims kicked off in earnest on Tuesday, when former Labour Cabinet minister Alan Milburn published a long-awaited review into youth unemployment — before being given a new post chairing a youth opportunities unit to help drive the reforms. He proposes changing the disability benefits young people are entitled to while giving them a legal right to education, employment or training. He also suggests that employers’ National Insurance contributions should be cut for 21-to-24-year-olds in the retail and hospitality sectors for five years. Advertisement Advertisement There’s a long way to go before MPs find out which of Milburn’s recommendations the government implements. A white paper and legislation are not due to be published until next year. Getting Labour MPs — many of whom are long-standing anti-poverty campaigners — to back plans which ultimately aim to cut Britain’s massive welfare bill will be no mean feat. Despite a huge majority in the House of Commons, Starmer was forced to roll back plans to reduce personal independence payments — which go to disabled people both in and out of work — after a well-organized campaign by senior Labour figures back in 2025. POLITICO runs through the key figures from the governing party whose views on the report — and critically Burnham’s eventual proposal — are worth paying attention to. 1) The committee chairs Treasury Committee Chair Meg Hillier and Work and Pensions Committee Chair Debbie Abrahams played a crucial role in halting some of Starmer’s welfare reforms. Hillier wrote an amendment to Starmer’s welfare plans which would have stopped the bill at its first hurdle. More than 100 Labour MPs from across the party signaled they would back it, forcing ministers to change course and promise any changes would only be made after a review by Disabilities Minister Stephen Timms, which is due later this month. Advertisement Advertisement Abrahams — who supported Hillier’s blocking amendment — was another key organizer of the welfare revolt under Starmer, and has repeatedly warned that reform should not take support away from those who need it most. Hillier said last week, after some of Milburn’s proposals were previewed in an interview in the Times newspaper, that he had “done some very good work on this” and she was “giving him a fair wind.” She said it was “quite radical and quite bold and quite right to be looking holistically at the person in the middle of this, not just about the money or the structure of the benefits.” On Tuesday, Abrahams described them as the “opportunity of a generation,” welcoming Milburn’s “rigorous analysis” on why young people become “NEETs” – not in education, employment or training. 2) The ministers Milburn’s proposals come with a price tag, making Chancellor John Healey a crucial figure to watch as Burnham finalizes his plans. The overall changes would cost £5.8 billion a year — offset by £6 billion in savings, Milburn suggests. Advertisement Advertisement Also sitting around the Cabinet table is Burnham’s de facto deputy, Louise Haigh, who helped organize the rebellion against Starmer’s welfare reforms. And Vicky Foxcroft, who quit as a government whip in June 2025, warning that cuts to PIP and Universal Credit should “not be part of the solution” to bringing down the welfare bill, is now a culture minister. All are now bound by collective responsibility, where ministers must not speak out openly against the government agenda. But every word they utter on welfare will be closely scrutinized for clues on exactly where the government might land. 3) The grandee Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown — who has long campaigned against poverty and inequality — is seen as an authority on welfare in the Labour Party. He parked the convention that ex-prime ministers try not to make life difficult for their successors in an interview with the New Statesman last year, reflecting on the “worrying issue” of reducing social security that left people “in poverty as a result.” Advertisement Advertisement He campaigned for — and lauded — the Starmer government’s move to abolish a two-child benefit cap. Any intervention by this ex-PM would be significant. 4) The wider rank and file The strength of feeling among other key backbench MPs who rebelled over Starmer’s plans will be an important barometer of how Burnham’s own reforms take shape. Marie Tidball — who has a congenital disability affecting all four of her limbs and strongly campaigned for changes to Starmer’s reforms behind the scenes — welcomed Milburn’s messaging that there “won’t be crude cuts to benefits.” Rachael Maskell, another vocal rebel, also welcomed the report, though warned employers should not “discriminate against young people being able to secure a job, not least if they experience severe anxiety or mental health challenges.” Mainstream — a soft left Labour faction of which Burnham was an early backer — said in a statement there is “much to welcome” in the review. However, the group’s interim council warned in its X post that the ambition “must not come at the expense of anyone already struggling to get by.” Advertisement Advertisement 5) The Starmerites Ministers who served under Starmer know just how hard welfare reform is — and their views on Burnham’s plans will grab attention. Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves is yet to comment on Milburn’s costly suggestions, but was busy defending her own record by highlighting a new report showing reduced levels of child poverty after she scrapped the two-child benefit cap. Liz Kendall — who was work and pensions secretary under Starmer —was keen to raise a lack of AI skills and experience that could affect NEETs.

https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/.text: It is a Harris tweed jacket. One family have cherished it for seven decades. The well-made blazer is a symbol of three men's dangerous dash for freedom and new lives in Manchester. Just eleven days after the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was brutally crushed the trio decided to leave their homeland for good. Under darkness on November 22nd András Lichtneker, György Zalavari and his cousin Jenő Poszavecz set off on their bikes from their homes in the village of Szepetnek. For three perilous days they rode and walked across Hungary to the Austrian border, sleeping in farm buildings, knowing that if they were caught they would be shot. After crossing into Austria they were helped by the Red Cross. The charity gave them clothes when they arrived in England. András was given the tweed jacket. The three were among an estimated 200,000 Hungarians who fled. About 2,500 Hungarians were killed in clashes during a revolt against the Soviet-controlled communist government of Hungary. The Hungarians had no freedom of speech and the secret police arrested anyone who spoke out against communism. Fearing the collapse of communist rule the Soviet Union responded by sending thousands of troops and tanks to Budapest on November 4th 1956. By November 11th the uprising was over. Many who attempted to flee were blocked and 26,000 were arrested, tried, and imprisoned. Some were executed. Now, to mark the 70th anniversary of their epic ride the families of two of the three men will travel to Hungary to retrace the escape route and make the same journey on bikes. András, who died in 2024 aged 89, will be represented by six family members, while György, now 91, will be represented by his son. The riding group will also include two Hungarian relatives of András. They will represent Jenő, who died in an industrial accident in the 1960s. András's son David Lichtneker, said: "Having heard many stories of the journey the three men made, the families of András and György felt the time was right to follow the approximately 120km route that they took. Using György’s recollections and video footage of András in which he shares his memories, the team will cycle to Lenti on the first day and head towards the border at Rönök on the second. "On the final day, they’ll join up with additional family members to walk the last 12km from the border to Gussing in Austria, where the three men were taken in by the Red Cross." Following their arrival in England in 1956, all three men settled in Manchester. András and György remained life-long friends, marrying Italian sisters and living on the same street just two houses away from each other. They still have relatives living in Szepetnek. David said: “They were riding for their lives. We want to honour their courage and determination – and celebrate the lives they went on to build in England.” The family members involved now live in Stretford , Preston, Marple Bridge and Cheshire. They intend stay as closely as possible to the route the three took even though some of the roads may not exist anymore. David said: "We know they went through a lot of fields and along dirt tracks in order to stay out of sight. They only decided to go the night before they left. He added: "Young men were disappearing from their village and being sent to Siberia. They didn’t want to be next and it was Gyorgy who instigated their escape. He’d already discussed it with Jeno, his cousin. It was by sheer chance that András went to visit them the day before, when they were preparing to leave. "When he found out what they were planning to do, he said he was going with them and they left the next morning at 5am, agreeing beforehand that if one them didn’t turn up, the others would leave without them. "They left with little more than the clothes they were wearing. They were hiding from the Russian army, mainly travelling under cover of darkness. If they had been discovered, they would have been shot. So they slept in barns and were helped by strangers along the way - a risk in itself. "At one point on the route, they started to argue about which way to go. András wanted to go one way, György wanted to go another way. They went the way György chose. They then heard gunshots from the direction Andras had chosen." On the first night, they knocked on the door of an old couple who let them sleep in their stable – with a cow – using straw for beds. The second day, there was deep snow. They had to push their bikes and managed to buy milk and bread along the way. They mainly avoided villages and went through countryside. "We know they had to abandon their bikes at one point and left them with some people who promised they would be returned to their village. Amazingly, that’s exactly what happened. "Eventually, they found another house and were lucky to find helpful people once again. At the next house they found, they discovered more people who were escaping, there were around ten or 12 of them in total. The locals helped them find the best way to go to the border. There were snipers at the border, it was incredible, it is like a book or a film. "They went through a forest to get into Austria – which wasn’t being patrolled by border guards. They soon arrived at a bus stop with a small terminal building, which was full of fellow refugees and they were picked up by buses," said David. They were dropped off at a small town, believed to be Gussing, and were taken to a cinema from where more buses arrived to take them to Graz – where they met three other young men from their village. A few days later, they were taken to another location in Austria, where they stayed for a week to ten days. They initially planned to go to the US, because Jenő had an uncle living there. But they were interviewed about the possibility of going to England and two days later they were on a train to Linz to go to the airport. They landed at a military airport in Kent and were given temporary accommodation in Dover Castle. They were then transferred to army barracks in Styal, Cheshire. Once in Styal, they were all given work at the same factory and started to settle down, socializing with members of a Hungarian social club. They also made friends with members of an Italian social club. Eventually, they went their separate ways to look for rented accommodation in Manchester. After working for ICI for a while, András found a job at Spiller’s and then moved to BOCM, which were both in Trafford Bar. He later worked for the Royal Mail. The first house he bought was in Old Trafford, before moving to Stretford in 1977, where he stayed for the rest of his life, bringing up his family. He is survived by his widow, Letizia, 91. György drove Greater Manchester buses for much of his working life. His first two houses were in Chorlton , before he moved to Stretford, where András, was just two doors away. He still lives there today. He sadly lost his wife Rosina in the early 2000s. Jenő worked for a transport company in Oldham , where he lived. He was tragically killed in an industrial accident in the mid 1960s. He is survived by a daughter. András married his Italian wife, Letizia, at St Alphonsus Church in Old Trafford and György married her sister Rosina at the same church. András had two daughters and a son; and György also had two daughters and a son. It was David's idea to retrace the journey the three made. He has called it Route 56 Revisited. Taking part in the bike ride will be Anna White, András's daughter, and her husband David, who live in Preston, and three of their four sons, grandsons of András - who carried the coffin at his funeral: Joseph of Leeds, Andrew (London) and James (Liverpool). György’s son who lives in Cheshire will also take part, plus David Lichtneker, originally from Stretford who now lives in the Netherlands and two Hungarian relatives of András who will represent Jenő. Others in the group who are travelling to Hungary include David’s wife who will be in the support vehicle and will take part in the walk to Gussing on the final day. András’ other daughter and her husband (who live in Marple Bridge) and their son (who lives in London) will meet up with the cyclists at the end of the second day. David said: "A museum in Hungary is interested in us giving them an album showing the life they all led after they arrived in England, their families, and work. They all moved to Manchester in 1956 and never left. "As it's the 70th anniversary we thought it might be the last chance we ever get to be together as a family. I intend to document it and will be taking photography equipment."
